section.title: The Transfiguration and the Call to Follow
section.sectionRationale: On the mountain the Father unveils the glory of His chosen Son and commands, Listen to Him. Coming down, the disciples fail before a demon, quarrel about greatness, and cannot grasp the coming cross. Then, at verse 51, the Gospel turns on its hinge: Jesus resolutely sets His face for Jerusalem, and the long travel narrative begins. The section closes with three would-be followers and the single-minded cost of the kingdom.
section.thesis: The transfigured Son whom the Father tells us to heed is the same Son who steadfastly walks toward the cross at Jerusalem, and to follow Him is to take that road with undivided, unlooking-back devotion.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the glory on the mountain and the Father's voice; the boy no one else could heal; the passion foretold amid an argument over greatness; the great hinge as Jesus sets out for Jerusalem; and the cost of following Him.

units.label: The glory on the mountain
units.note: This is My Son; listen to Him

verses.text: About eight days after Jesus had said these things, He took with Him Peter, John, and James, and went up on a mountain to pray.
And as He was praying, the appearance of His face changed, and His clothes became radiantly white.
Suddenly two men, Moses and Elijah, began talking with Jesus.
They appeared in {{doxa|glory}} and spoke about His {{exodos|departure}}, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
Meanwhile Peter and his companions were overcome by sleep, but when they awoke, they saw Jesus’ glory and the two men standing with Him.

As Moses and Elijah were leaving, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us put up three shelters, one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (He did not know what he was saying.)
While Peter was speaking, a cloud appeared and enveloped them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud.
And a voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is My Son, whom I have {{eklegomai|chosen}}. Listen to Him!”
After the voice had spoken, only Jesus was present with them. The disciples kept this to themselves, and in those days they did not tell anyone what they had seen.

units.label: The boy no one else could heal
units.note: an unbelieving generation, and the greatness of God

verses.text: The next day, when they came down from the mountain, Jesus was met by a large crowd.
Suddenly a man in the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg You to look at my son, for he is my only child.
A spirit keeps seizing him, and he screams abruptly. It throws him into convulsions so that he foams at the mouth. It keeps mauling him and rarely departs from him.
I begged Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.”
“O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.”
Even while the boy was approaching, the demon slammed him to the ground in a convulsion. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.

units.label: The passion foretold, and the argument over greatness

verses.text: And they were all astonished at the greatness of God. While everyone was marveling at all that Jesus was doing, He said to His disciples,
“Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.”
But they did not understand this statement. It was veiled from them so that they could not comprehend it, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.
Then an argument started among the disciples as to which of them would be the greatest.
But Jesus, knowing the thoughts of their hearts, had a little child stand beside Him.
And He said to them, “Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes the One who sent Me. For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest.”
“Master,” said John, “we saw someone driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.”
“Do not stop him,” Jesus replied, “for whoever is not against you is for you.”

units.label: He set His face for Jerusalem
units.note: the great hinge of the Gospel

verses.text: As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem.
He sent messengers on ahead, who went into a village of the Samaritans to make arrangements for Him.
But the people there refused to welcome Him, because He was heading for Jerusalem.
When the disciples James and John saw this, they asked, “Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?”
But Jesus turned and rebuked them.
And He and His disciples went on to another village.

units.label: The cost of following
units.note: no one who looks back is fit

verses.text: As they were walking along the road, someone said to Jesus, “I will follow You wherever You go.”
Jesus replied, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.”
Then He said to another man, “{{akoloutheo|Follow}} Me.” The man replied, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.”
But Jesus told him, “Let the dead bury their own dead. You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.”
Still another said, “I will follow You, Lord; but first let me bid farewell to my family.”
Then Jesus declared, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

exodos.gloss: A going out, a departure, an exodus. Luke alone records that Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus' exodos, His departure to be accomplished at Jerusalem. The word ties His death, resurrection, and ascension to the great exodus out of Egypt: Jesus will lead a new rescue through His own death.

doxa.gloss: Glory, splendor, the radiant weight of God's presence. On the mountain the veil is lifted and the disciples glimpse the doxa that belongs to the Son, a foretaste of the glory into which He will enter through the cross and beyond it.

eklegomai.gloss: To choose, to select. The Father names Jesus My Son, whom I have chosen, echoing the Servant of Isaiah 42:1 whom God upholds and delights in. The One chosen and beloved is the One we are commanded to heed above Moses and Elijah.

akoloutheo.gloss: To follow, to accompany as a disciple, to walk the same road. Jesus' call, Follow Me, is a summons to travel His way to Jerusalem, and the closing sayings show that this following allows no rival first claim and no looking back.

basic.context: Jesus takes Peter, John, and James up a mountain to pray, and there His face and clothing blaze with glory. Moses and Elijah appear and speak of His departure, His coming death at Jerusalem. The Father's voice declares Him the chosen Son and commands, Listen to Him. Coming down, the disciples cannot drive a demon out of a boy, they argue about who is greatest, and they fail to grasp Jesus' plain word that He will be handed over. Then at verse 51 everything turns: Jesus sets His face for Jerusalem, and the road to the cross begins. Three would-be followers meet Him on the way, and He tells each that the kingdom asks everything.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the mountain and the road together. The glory of verses 28 to 36 is not detached from the cross; Moses and Elijah speak precisely of His departure, and the same Son revealed in glory is the Son who walks to Jerusalem in verse 51. The travel narrative that opens here governs the next ten chapters of Luke, so this passage is a doorway, not a detour.
basic.originalLanguages: Three Greek words anchor the scene. Moses and Elijah speak of Jesus' exodos, His departure, tying His death to the exodus. The disciples see His doxa, His glory. The Father names Him the Son whom He has chosen, eklegomai, the delighted-in Servant. And the road ends with a call to akoloutheo, to follow, with nothing held back.
basic.typology: Moses the lawgiver and Elijah the prophet meet Jesus and then fade, leaving only the Son; the law and the prophets point to Him and give way to Him. His exodos fulfills the pattern of the first exodus, a greater rescue won not from Egypt but from sin and death.
basic.christ: Jesus is the transfigured, chosen Son of the Father, greater than Moses and Elijah, the One we must heed. Yet His glory is bound to His suffering: He speaks of being delivered into the hands of men, and He sets His face for Jerusalem to accomplish His departure there. The mountain gives a glimpse of the glory the cross will open.
basic.god: The Father Himself speaks from the cloud, identifying His chosen Son and commanding that we listen to Him. God is the one who unveils glory, who ordains the departure at Jerusalem, and whose greatness astonishes the crowd even as His Son walks toward the cross.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Peter 1 recalls the majesty on the holy mountain and the voice from heaven. Isaiah 42 supplies the chosen Servant. Malachi 4 promises Elijah. Philippians 2 traces the same path from self-emptying obedience to exaltation.
basic.oneStory: The chosen Son is unveiled in glory, then turns His face toward Jerusalem to accomplish the departure that rescues His people. Following Him means walking that same road with undivided hearts, for the way to glory runs through the cross.

context.literary:
Luke 9:28 to 62 is a hinge, and its structure shows it. Verses 28 to 36 are a scene of glory on a mountain, verses 37 to 50 are a descent into failure in the valley, and verses 51 to 62 are the start of a journey. The three movements are held together by the words 'Jerusalem' and 'departure.' On the mountain, Moses and Elijah speak of the 'departure' that Jesus will 'accomplish at Jerusalem,' verse 31. In the valley the Son of Man is 'about to be delivered into the hands of men,' verse 44, and the disciples cannot grasp it. At verse 51 He 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem.' Luke has made the cross the destination of the whole chapter before a single step toward it is taken.

There is a deliberate contrast between the mountain and the valley. On the mountain three disciples are overcome by sleep and wake to glory, and in the valley the disciples cannot cast out a demon. On the mountain the Father says 'Listen to Him!', and in the valley the disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask. They have the vision and the voice, and they still do not hear. The sequence of failures that follows, an exorcism that fails, a quarrel about greatness, a rebuke of an outsider and a wish to call down fire, is a catalogue of the reasons the Father had to say 'Listen.'

Verse 51 begins what is usually called the travel narrative, which runs to Luke 19:27 or 19:44 depending on how it is counted. Almost nothing of this material is in Mark or Matthew in the same form, and it contains many of the best-known parables. Luke has built a long journey so that the reader will go up to Jerusalem with Jesus slowly, and with teaching on every step.

The final unit, verses 57 to 62, gives three short exchanges, each with the same pattern: a would-be follower, a condition, and a reply that raises the stakes. They are neatly graded. The first promises too much, the second asks for a delay, and the third wants a farewell. Together with Jesus' own example of resolute purpose they define discipleship as following Him to the place He is going.
context.historical:
Luke does not name the mountain. Tradition has pointed to Mount Tabor, and some scholars have favoured Hermon, but the text gives no name, and the emphasis is on what happened, not where. 'About eight days' is Luke's way of saying a week later, and he does not use the language of 'six days' found in Matthew and Mark; it is a different way of counting the same interval. Jesus takes Peter, John and James, and Luke tells us they went up to pray.

The scene is laden with Israel's memory. Moses had gone up Sinai, and the glory of the LORD settled on the mountain in a cloud, Exodus 24:15 to 18, and when he came down his face was radiant, Exodus 34:29. Elijah had met God on Horeb, the same mountain, and had been taken up in a whirlwind. Peter's proposal for three 'shelters,' the tents used at the Feast of Tabernacles, may show that he reached for the nearest religious category, a festival booth, as he tried to prolong the moment. The cloud that 'enveloped' them was the sign of God's presence over the tent of meeting, Exodus 40:34 to 35, and it brings the fear that the Israelites also felt.

Ancient Jews expected Moses and Elijah to return. Deuteronomy 18:15 promised a prophet like Moses, and Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah before the day of the LORD. A first-century hearer would have understood their appearance as the arrival of something decisive.

In verse 51 'the day of His ascension' translates a phrase meaning the days of His being taken up, which covers His death, resurrection and ascension together. The Samaritans in verse 53 refused hospitality because He was heading for Jerusalem. The old quarrel between Samaritans and Jews over the proper place of worship lay behind this, and a pilgrim to Jerusalem was a symbol of the opposing side. James and John's desire to call down fire is a reference to Elijah, 2 Kings 1:10, and to the long memory of judgment on a hostile town.

On the road, 'foxes have dens' is a plain contrast in a country where a rabbi might expect lodging. 'Let the dead bury their own dead' touches on a heavy obligation. Burying a parent was among the strongest duties in Jewish life, and the third exchange recalls Elisha's request in 1 Kings 19:20 to say goodbye to his parents.
context.canonical:
The transfiguration sits where law, prophets and gospel meet. Moses stands for the Law, Elijah for the Prophets, and the voice from the cloud declares that neither is the last word. Luke 24:44 will later say that everything written about Him in 'the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms' had to be fulfilled, and here the first two are present. Malachi 4:4 to 5 closes the Old Testament by naming exactly these two figures, 'Remember the law of My servant Moses' and 'I will send you Elijah the prophet,' and Luke sets them beside the Son.

The voice takes the vocabulary of Scripture. 'This is My Son' calls up Psalm 2:7. 'Whom I have chosen' recalls Isaiah 42:1, 'My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights.' And 'Listen to Him!' is the command about the prophet like Moses in Deuteronomy 18:15, 'You must listen to him.' In a single line the Father identifies the King of the psalms, the Servant of Isaiah and the Prophet of Moses, and identifies all three as one. The other Gospels tell the story in Matthew 17 and Mark 9. The title 'Chosen One' returns in Luke 23:35, where the rulers mock Him on the cross.

The event is remembered by the apostles. Peter writes, 'we were eyewitnesses of His majesty,' and recalls that the voice came 'from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain,' 2 Peter 1:16 to 18. John's prologue, 'we have seen His glory,' John 1:14, may also look back to this experience. Hebrews 1:1 to 2 gives the doctrine, that God who spoke through the prophets 'has spoken to us by His Son.'

The 'two men' are not the last to appear in Luke. Two men in radiant apparel stand beside the women at the empty tomb, Luke 24:4, and two men stand by the disciples at the ascension in Acts 1:10. The Father's command to listen is picked up in Acts 3:22, where Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18 of Jesus.

The travel narrative that starts at verse 51 echoes Isaiah's Servant, 'I have set My face like flint,' Isaiah 50:7, as the Servant is determined in the face of suffering.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wanted his readers to hold together two things that the disciples could not: that Jesus is the glorious Son of God, and that He is walking to a cross. The mountain tells them who He is, and the road tells them what He will do. If either were missing, the Gospel would be distorted into a triumph without suffering or a martyrdom without glory.

He also meant to tell them what the Father wants from them. In the whole account of the transfiguration there is one command, and it is not 'build' or 'admire.' It is 'Listen to Him!' Luke immediately shows what refusing to listen looks like: the disciples fail to understand a plain prediction, argue over greatness, and want to destroy a village. A reader of this section is asked to measure his own hearing against the Father's command.

And he meant them to see that the call to follow is real and costly. The three men on the road are presented honestly. Luke does not say what they decided. The question stays open to the reader, who is meant to put himself in their place. The answer Jesus gives to each, that the Son of Man has no home, that the kingdom takes priority over even the most sacred duties, and that no looking back is permitted, is meant for every reader who would walk the road behind Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The mountain is a unique revelation to three witnesses and is not a pattern for seeking experiences. Peter's wish to stay is gently called ignorance, 'He did not know what he was saying,' and the Father's reply redirects him from the vision to the Son's words. The text does not teach that Christians should look for transfiguration moments, and it warns against treating the glory as a place to stay. What it commands is listening.

The failures in the valley are described to us, not endorsed. The disciples' argument over greatness, John's attempt to stop the stranger and the wish for fire from heaven are examples of what to avoid, and Jesus rebukes each in turn. Equally, His rebuke of James and John should not be read as a general rule for how to treat hostile towns. It corrects a spirit of vengeance in those who follow the Lamb.

The three sayings on the road are prescriptive for disciples, but they are hard sayings, and they need to be read in their context. 'Let the dead bury their own dead' does not abolish respect for parents, which the law itself commands. It says that when the kingdom calls, nothing is allowed to take its place. The point is the priority of Jesus' call, to be applied as a matter of loyalty, not as a command to neglect family.

debates.question: What did the Father mean by naming Jesus the Son whom He has chosen?

views.label: An echo of the chosen Servant
views.case: The wording recalls Isaiah 42:1, My chosen one in whom My soul delights, casting Jesus as the Servant who will suffer to save; this fits the talk of His departure at Jerusalem.

views.label: A declaration of unique divine sonship
views.case: Set beside the fading Moses and Elijah, the words single Jesus out as the beloved and only Son to be heeded above the law and the prophets, in continuity with His baptism.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge: the chosen, beloved Son is also the suffering Servant, so His glory and His cross are held together, and He alone is to be obeyed.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean by 'Let the dead bury their own dead'?

views.label: The spiritually dead bury the physically dead
views.case: The most common reading takes the first 'dead' as people who do not yet have life in the kingdom, and the second as the man's father. On this view Jesus says that those who are outside the kingdom can handle funerals, while the follower must go and proclaim the kingdom. It fits the contrast with 'You, however, go and proclaim,' and the way Luke and John use death and life of those who have not responded to God.

views.label: The father was not yet dead
views.case: Some suggest that 'let me bury my father' meant 'let me wait until my father dies and then follow you,' so the man was asking for an open-ended delay and not a few days to attend a funeral. This would explain why he was nowhere near the grave, since a dead father would normally be buried the same day. The case depends on a reading of the idiom that we cannot confirm from the text itself.

views.label: A deliberate overstatement
views.case: A third approach takes the saying as a vivid exaggeration meant to shock. Jesus is not telling anyone to dishonour parents, which the law commands, but pushing his point to the extreme that the kingdom's claim outranks even the most weighty family duty. This fits the other hard sayings of the section, such as the hand on the plough, and Jesus' own example of setting His face to Jerusalem. On every reading the bearing is the same: the call of the kingdom is first.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is exodos in verse 31. Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about His 'departure,' using the word that Greek-speaking Jews used as the name of the book of Exodus, the great going-out from Egypt. Luke chooses it over words for death, such as thanatos, and the choice invites the reader to think of what the first exodus involved: a lamb, a blood-marked door, a crossing through water and a journey to a promised land. The verb 'accomplish' is plēroun, 'to fulfil,' literally to fill up, and it suggests that the departure is not an accident of history but a task assigned and completed. Peter uses the same noun of his own death in 2 Peter 1:15, which shows that the word was used among the early Christians of an event with a meaning beyond itself.

Luke avoids the verb that Matthew and Mark use of the transfiguration, metamorphoō, 'to be changed in form,' perhaps to spare Greek readers a word with associations of pagan gods changing shape. He says instead that 'the appearance of His face changed,' heteron, and that His clothing became leukos exastraptōn, 'brilliantly white, flashing like lightning.' The word for the glory they saw is doxa, which in the Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew kavod, the weighty radiance of God's presence. The sleep that overcame the disciples is described as heaviness, bebarēmenoi hypnō, and the same kind of heaviness will fall on them in Gethsemane, Luke 22:45, so the disciples who saw the glory will be found sleeping in the dark.

In verse 34 the cloud 'enveloped' them, episkiazō, to overshadow. Luke used this very verb of the Spirit and the power of the Most High overshadowing Mary, Luke 1:35, and the Greek Old Testament uses it of the cloud settling on the tent of meeting, Exodus 40:35. It is the verb of God's presence coming to dwell. The Father's voice names the Son eklelegmenos, 'chosen,' a perfect passive participle that points to a choice made and standing. The word belongs to Isaiah's Servant, Isaiah 42:1, and it is the same word the rulers use on the cross, ho eklektos, 'the Chosen One.' The command autou akouete, 'listen to him,' is a present imperative, meaning keep on listening, and it echoes the command about the prophet like Moses in Deuteronomy 18:15.

In the valley Jesus calls His hearers a genea apistos kai diestrammenē, an 'unbelieving and perverse generation,' verse 41, borrowing the language of Moses' song, 'a perverse and crooked generation,' Deuteronomy 32:5. The scene also echoes Exodus 32, where Moses came down from the mountain to find the people faithless. Luke notes that the boy is monogenēs, an 'only child,' verse 38, the word he uses of Jairus' daughter and the widow's son. Jesus then 'gave him back to his father.'

Verse 51 is the great hinge. 'Resolutely set out' is a literal 'he set his face,' to prosōpon autou estērisen, a Hebrew idiom for firm determination. Isaiah 50:7 uses the image of a face like flint, and it carries the idea of someone who will not turn aside. The phrase translated 'the day of His ascension' contains the noun analēmpsis, 'being taken up,' which gathers up cross, resurrection and ascension in one word. The followers' replies on the road use akoloutheō, 'to follow,' the word for a disciple. In verse 62 the one who looks back is not euthetos, 'fit' or 'well suited,' for the kingdom.

typology.type: Moses on the mountain, Exodus 24 and 34
typology.fulfillment: Moses went up into the cloud on Sinai, and the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire, Exodus 24:15 to 18. When he came down his face was radiant, Exodus 34:29. Luke shows Jesus going up to pray, His face changing, a cloud descending and a voice speaking. The correspondence is intended: Israel's lawgiver is replaced as the centre of attention by the Son. In Moses the glory was reflected after he met God; in Jesus it shines from within. The type falls short because Moses had to veil his face and lead the people toward a promised land he could not enter, while the Son has the glory as His own and brings His people in, 2 Corinthians 3:7 to 18.

typology.type: The exodus and the greater departure
typology.fulfillment: The topic of the conversation is the exodos that Jesus is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Israel's exodus rescued a people from slavery through a lamb, a night of judgment and a crossing of the sea, and it formed the basis of Israel's identity. At Jerusalem Jesus will accomplish the greater rescue, and the Gospels place His death at Passover. The correspondence is liberation by substitution. The escalation is that the enemy is sin and death, not Pharaoh, and the destination is not Canaan but the Father. The type falls short in that the first exodus left Israel's hearts unchanged, and the new one gives a new heart, Ezekiel 36:26 and Hebrews 8:10.

typology.type: Elijah and Elisha, the fire and the plough
typology.fulfillment: Elijah called down fire on hostile soldiers, 2 Kings 1:10, and James and John want to do the same to a Samaritan village. Jesus turns and rebukes them. Elisha was called while ploughing and asked to kiss his parents goodbye, to which Elijah answered 'Go on back,' 1 Kings 19:20. Jesus does not permit even that. The correspondence is that the Son stands in the line of Elijah, as the one who calls disciples. The escalation is that the Son's call is more demanding because His mission is greater, and His mercy is greater because He has come to save and not to burn. The type falls short in that Elijah was a prophet who passed his mantle on, and Jesus gives His Spirit.

typology.type: The Servant who sets his face, Isaiah 50:7
typology.fulfillment: The Servant says, 'I have set My face like flint, and I know that I will not be put to shame.' The Gospel picks up the image in verse 51. The correspondence is determination in the face of coming suffering, with trust that the Lord will vindicate. In Isaiah the Servant is struck and spat upon, and Luke's readers know that Jesus will be. The escalation is the geography: the face is set toward a specific city, and the journey takes up ten chapters. The type falls short only in the sense that Isaiah leaves the Servant unnamed, while Luke names Him as the Son whom the Father has chosen.

study.christ:
The transfiguration reveals the identity of Christ and the cross reveals His mission, and Luke puts them in the same breath. The Father calls Him 'My Son, whom I have chosen,' and at once the topic of conversation is His departure. The glory is not a detour. It is a revelation of who is going to Jerusalem, so that the disciples, and the readers, will not mistake the cross for a defeat.

Christ is greater than Moses and Elijah. This is not a matter of rank among prophets only. When Moses and Elijah are 'leaving,' Peter wants to keep all three, and the Father answers by taking the other two away: 'only Jesus was present with them.' The Law and the Prophets point to Him and give way to Him, which is what Luke 24:27 means when the risen Christ explains to the two on the road 'what was said in all the Scriptures concerning Himself.' Hebrews makes the same point, that God spoke by the prophets in many ways and now 'by His Son,' Hebrews 1:1 to 2.

He is the Prophet like Moses. The Father's command, 'Listen to Him,' draws on Deuteronomy 18:15, the promise of a prophet like Moses whom the people must hear. Peter says so in Acts 3:22. To listen to Jesus is to obey the whole counsel of God, because He is the one to whom the Law and Prophets bear witness.

He is the Servant who determines to suffer. Verse 51 shows Him acting with His whole will, with no sign of reluctance. Unlike the disciples who do not understand, the Lord moves toward the cross knowing what it means. Paul would later say that He 'became obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8, and 'therefore God exalted Him,' verse 9. The order in Luke is the same, with glory shown, then the road to suffering, then exaltation.

And He is the Son of Man who has nowhere to lay His head. The reply to the first would-be follower says that the one who holds all authority has no house on earth. The One who is revealed in glory lives without a home so that others may have one in His Father's house. The foxes and birds, which have dens and nests, are better housed than the Lord of heaven. Here Christ's glory and humility are held in a single sentence.

There should be caution about overreading the details. The eight days are not a coded number, the three shelters are not allegories, and the cloud does not need to be matched to a doctrine of the Trinity beyond what the text says. The firm line is the one the apostles drew, as in 2 Peter 1:16 to 18, where the event is a confirmation of Christ's majesty and the Father's honour. What the passage gives us is the Son in His glory, a voice that commands that we hear Him, and a face set toward the cross.
study.god:
The God of the transfiguration speaks. In a scene packed with visible wonder, the Father's contribution is a sentence, and it is the point of the whole episode. God is the God who identifies His Son, who tells people what to do with Him, and who does so from within a cloud that both reveals and conceals. He is the God of Sinai again, a God of glory and holiness whom the disciples find frightening, and yet this glory belongs to a man who has been eating and sleeping among them.

This is the God of the Trinity at work. The Son is transfigured while He prays, the Father speaks from the cloud, and the cloud is the sign of the Spirit's overshadowing presence, as it was over Mary in Luke 1:35. Luke does not state a doctrine. He shows the Father, the Son and the presence of God in a single scene, so that later Christian teaching on one God in three persons finds its ground in what the Gospel narrates and does not need to be imposed on it.

God is the one who ordains the departure. Moses and Elijah talk about what Jesus 'was about to accomplish,' and the verb implies a plan that is already under way. The cross is not a mistake that interrupts the Father's plan, and it is not a tragedy that surprises Him. It is the work He has sent the Son to do. At the same time, the Father is neither cruel nor distant: He honours the Son in public before the road begins, and He gives three friends a glimpse of what it is for.

God is patient with slow disciples. The Twelve fail in almost every way in the verses that follow the mountain, and yet there is no word of dismissal. The Lord corrects, teaches, and walks on with them. This is how God treats those He has chosen. He is also firm on certain points. He does not allow the disciples to turn mercy into judgment, as with the Samaritan village, and He does not accept half-hearted discipleship.

He is the God who calls and gives the call a price. The three men on the road discover that the kingdom does not accommodate a rival claim. This is not harshness; it is the nature of a King whose dominion is everlasting. And since He is the God who sets His own face toward Jerusalem, He asks nothing of His followers that He has not done Himself.

For worship, the chapter combines awe and obedience. The disciples' fear in the cloud is the right response to glory, but Peter's impulse to build something is checked. Worship in Luke 9 is not the capture of a mountaintop moment, it is to listen to the Son. It also asks us to come down from the mountain and meet the boy in the valley, because the God who shows glory also heals the child and gives him back to his father.

crossReferences.note: The glory of the LORD settles on Sinai in a cloud, and Moses enters it. Luke's scene, with a mountain, a cloud, a glory and an entrance into the cloud, is built from the same pieces. The disciples are in the position of Israel at the foot of the mountain, except that the glory now stands among them in a man.

Moses came down from Sinai with a radiant face, which he did not know. Jesus' face is changed as He prays, and the glory comes from Him. The echo shows the greatness of what Luke describes, and the contrast shows that Moses' glory was borrowed from his meeting with God while Jesus' is His own.

God promises to raise up a prophet like Moses, and the people must listen to him. The Father's command at the transfiguration, 'Listen to Him!', is this promise brought to its fulfilment. Peter later quotes the passage of Jesus in Acts 3:22, so the early church recognised the link.

The Servant is God's Chosen One, in whom His soul delights, and the Spirit rests on Him. The Father's phrase 'whom I have chosen' draws on this verse. It identifies the Son as the Servant who will bring justice, and it prepares the reader to expect that His way will involve suffering.

The last words of the Old Testament tell Israel to remember the law of Moses and promise that Elijah will come before the day of the LORD. Moses and Elijah appear together on the mountain, which reads like the book's final verses coming true in person. They stand aside for the one the law and the prophets were waiting for.

Peter looks back on the mountain as an eyewitness. He says they did not follow fables, but saw His majesty and heard the voice from heaven. The apostle regards the transfiguration as the guarantee of the message he preaches, and it confirms that Luke is describing a real event.

At the tomb two men in radiant apparel stand beside the women, just as two men in glory stood with Jesus on the mountain. The mountain's glory is a preview of the resurrection, and the repeated 'two men' invites the reader to link the departure of verse 31 with the empty tomb.

The Servant sets His face like flint, trusting that He will not be put to shame. Jesus' resolute set of His face toward Jerusalem in Luke 9:51 uses the same picture of determination. It shows that the journey is voluntary, grounded in trust in the Father, and shaped by the Servant's pattern.

Elijah calls down fire from heaven on the soldiers who came for him. James and John want to do the same to the Samaritan village. Jesus rebukes them, which shows that He is not simply a new Elijah. His mission is to save, and His kingdom does not advance by fire.

Elisha is called from the plough and asks to kiss his parents goodbye, and Elijah allows him to go back. The third would-be follower asks for the same, and Jesus answers that no one who looks back is fit for the kingdom. The comparison shows that the call of Jesus is more urgent than even a prophet's.

God spoke by the prophets in many ways and now has spoken by His Son. This is the doctrine behind the voice from the cloud. When Moses and Elijah leave and only Jesus remains, the New Testament's claim is that God's final word has been spoken in the Son.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God has desired to dwell with His people. In Eden He walked in the garden, and when the garden was lost He met them at Sinai in a cloud, then in the tabernacle where the glory filled the tent, Exodus 40:34. The people could not approach, and Moses had to veil his face. The transfiguration is a moment in that long story where the glory is seen on a human face and the cloud covers people who are not destroyed. It is a sign that the God who hid Himself is coming near.

Israel's history had told the same story in a lower key. The Law was given on a mountain, and the prophets, of whom Elijah is the greatest, called the people back to it. But both ended in the same place, a people who would not listen, Deuteronomy 32:5. The valley scene repeats it in miniature, and Luke's careful echo of Moses' words shows that the problem of Israel's hearing is the problem of the disciples' hearing. The remedy that the Father gives is the person of the Son: 'Listen to Him!'

The departure that Moses and Elijah discuss is the heart of the story. The exodus from Egypt was the shape of redemption, and the cross will be its fulfilment. Jesus sets out for Jerusalem knowing what it holds, and the rest of Luke is the journey. Because He goes, the way is opened that Genesis 3 closed. The Gospel ends with a risen Lord taken up into heaven, Luke 24:51, and the one who set His face to Jerusalem has finished what He set out to do.

The call to follow is the church's story. The three who spoke on the road, and the many who read about them, are asked to leave behind security, delay and a divided heart. This is the shape of the new people of God, who are the church of Acts and then of every age, following the Son toward a kingdom that does not yet appear.

The story ends with the glory that the three saw for a moment becoming the permanent condition of the world. Revelation 21:23 says the city has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and the Lamb is its lamp. 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. What the disciples glimpsed on a mountain, His people will see without a cloud. And the voice that said 'Listen to Him' will be answered by a people who do.

quiz.q: What did Moses and Elijah discuss with Jesus on the mountain?

options.text: His departure, His coming death, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
options.note: Luke 9:31 states they spoke of His exodos, His departure at Jerusalem.

options.text: The glory that Jesus would receive after His suffering.
options.note: Glory is truly in view, but the text specifies they spoke of His departure at Jerusalem.

options.text: How to build the three shelters Peter suggested.
options.note: Peter's shelters were his confused idea; the conversation was about His departure, not the shelters.

options.text: Plans to overthrow Rome by force.
options.note: Nothing of the sort; they spoke of His death, not political revolt.

quiz.q: What did the Father's voice from the cloud command?

options.text: This is My Son, whom I have chosen; listen to Him.
options.note: Luke 9:35 gives the Father's words identifying and commanding obedience to the Son.

options.text: To honor Moses and Elijah alongside Jesus.
options.note: Moses and Elijah appear, but the point is that only the Son remains and must be heard, not that all three are equal.

options.text: To keep the vision secret forever.
options.note: The disciples did keep it to themselves then, but the Father's command was to listen to the Son, not a rule of permanent secrecy.

options.text: To build a temple on the mountain.
options.note: No such command was given; the voice pointed to the Son.

quiz.q: What is the significance of Luke 9:51?

options.text: Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem, the great hinge where the journey to the cross begins.
options.note: Verse 51 opens Luke's long travel narrative toward Jerusalem and the cross.

options.text: Jesus decided to visit Jerusalem for a feast like any pilgrim.
options.note: He did go up to Jerusalem, but the verse marks a deliberate, cross-bound resolve, not an ordinary pilgrimage.

options.text: Jesus went to Jerusalem to be crowned an earthly king.
options.note: He goes toward a throne, but by way of the cross, not an earthly coronation.

options.text: Jesus gave up His mission and turned back.
options.note: The opposite: He set His face firmly toward Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach about following Him at the end of the chapter?

options.text: Following Him allows no rival first claim and no looking back once the hand is on the plow.
options.note: Luke 9:57-62 shows the single-minded cost of following Jesus.

options.text: Following Him is costly and may leave a disciple without earthly comforts.
options.note: True of verse 58, but the fuller point across the three sayings is undivided, unlooking-back devotion.

options.text: Following Him means first settling all family duties before starting.
options.note: Jesus actually refuses to let even a funeral or farewell take first place over the kingdom.

options.text: Following Him requires nothing and costs nothing.
options.note: Contrary to the passage, which stresses the full cost of discipleship.

quiz.q: How does the transfiguration relate to the cross in Luke's telling?

options.text: The glory and the cross are bound together; the chosen Son revealed in glory is the One who walks to Jerusalem to die.
options.note: The glory scene itself speaks of His departure, and verse 51 sends Him to the cross.

options.text: The transfiguration proves Jesus is glorious, and the cross is a later, separate event.
options.note: Both are true events, but Luke deliberately ties them together rather than separating them.

options.text: The transfiguration cancels the need for the cross.
options.note: The glory does not replace the cross; it frames His death as a chosen accomplishment.

options.text: The transfiguration shows Jesus avoiding suffering.
options.note: He does the opposite, setting out for the very city where He will suffer.

questions: The Father's command was simple: listen to Him. In a noisy week, what would it look like to actually give the Son the last word over Moses, Elijah, and every other voice?
Jesus came down from glory straight into a crowd, a failed exorcism, and a squabble about greatness. How does His willingness to enter our mess encourage you today?
At verse 51 Jesus set His face for Jerusalem, knowing what waited there. Where is God asking you for that kind of steady resolve rather than a wavering start?
To one man Jesus said follow Me, and named a good thing, a burial, that could not come first. What good thing are you tempted to let take first place over Him?
No one who looks back is fit for the kingdom. What are you tempted to keep glancing back toward, and what would undivided following look like instead?

translationNotes.note: Departure translates the Greek exodos. The word deliberately recalls Israel's exodus, presenting Jesus' death, resurrection, and ascension as the true and greater rescue accomplished at Jerusalem.

Whom I have chosen follows the earliest manuscripts; a number of later manuscripts read My beloved Son, harmonizing with Matthew 17:5. The BSB footnote records the variant. Either way the Father identifies and vindicates His Son.

Some later manuscripts add that James and John wished to call fire just as Elijah did, and that Jesus said they did not know what spirit they were of, and that the Son of Man came to save. The BSB places these in footnotes as they are absent from the earliest witnesses.
